title: DLSJ: closed-loop defect sorting on a Core Ultra laptop
tagline: A VLA picks every brick, an NPU detector reads it while the wrist spins it, and the arm sorts it. Perceive, detect, reason, act and optimise, all on one Intel Core Ultra Series 3 laptop.

pipeline.what: Top camera: YOLO brick detector finds the bricks left on the table and the plates; the next brick's colour becomes the VLA prompt.
MolmoAct2 (fine-tuned, OpenVINO INT8/FP16 + real-time chunking) picks the brick; the gripper reading confirms the grasp.
The same VLA brings the brick to the inspection camera; the spin starts when the arm settles.
The wrist rolls the brick through ~180 deg; the held-brick YOLO (v5, plain / marked) reads ~61 frames, ~4 ms each.
Evidence rule over all frames: marked needs enough confident marked frames, plain needs >= 80 % plain; uncertain -> re-spin -> defective.
Plain -> yellow plate, marked or uncertain -> purple plate; then straight on to the next brick.
PyTorch -> OpenVINO, INT8, RTC: 34x faster and 36x less energy per action chunk than the stock baseline.

bullets: Three phases per demo, each with its own prompt: pick up the <colour> brick, bring it to the inspection camera, place it in the <colour> bowl.
Auto-exposure and white balance locked on every camera; the cameras never move.
Data collection is built into the dashboard: label the brick, press Spin & save, and every crop is stored for retraining.
caveats: Older-calibration episodes were recorded before a recalibration and are not in the current fine-tune.

bullets: LoRA fine-tune of AI2's MolmoAct2 (already trained on SO-100/101) with our three-stage prompts.
Isaac Lab digital twin of the station: fitted servo response, fin-ray gripper, camera calibration (table-level error 2.7 -> 0.4 cm), deployment drift.
DICE-RL grasp residual: a small, bounded correction (+-3.5 cm, +-10 deg wrist) on the pick stage, trained with the real 8k model in the loop; deployable live as off / shadow / on.
Weight-space programming: an experimental wrist-edit of the 8k checkpoint (2.84 deg, not yet arm-tested).
caveats: The 7.4 -> 14.8 % residual result uses a scripted stand-in base in sim, not the real policy.
The DICE-RL residual's sim result is not published yet; 58 % is the prior-only baseline.
Robustness guarantees in sim: not yet measured.

sections.title: Runtime optimisation
sections.lead: Same 60 recorded frames, stock PyTorch vs what runs on the robot: OpenVINO on the Arc iGPU, INT8 weights, real-time chunking.

tables.title: Baseline vs now
rows: never idle (chunk lands before the queue runs dry)

tables.title: What each step bought
rows: PyTorch -> OpenVINO on the Arc iGPU
10,770 -> 362 ms (PyTorch on the GPU crashed the device)
+27 ms per call, no stalls; hand-off jump 2.6 -> 1.2 deg
YOLO on the NPU, perception only when needed
~4-6 ms per frame; servo-read errors gone
61 frames in 8.2 s vs 12 frames in 11.2 s

bullets: Device split: VLA on the Arc GPU, held-brick YOLO on the NPU, cameras and the 30 Hz control loop on the CPU.
The GPU draws a little more power while running (38.7 W vs 31.8 W package) but finishes each chunk 44x sooner.
caveats: Baseline is the zero-shot model; fine-tuning doesn't change the compute.
The power run's baseline took 13.7 s per chunk (warm machine) vs 10.8 s in the latency run.
The robot currently runs the FP16 export of the same model (~360 ms per chunk); INT8 is the benchmarked configuration.
